items.title: Claude Code 3.0 (All Upgrades Explained): You don't KNOW about THESE CRAZY NEW FEATURES YET!
items.summary:
Thank you to TestSprite for sponsoring this video: https://www.testsprite.com/?via=aicodingki-dw
Github repo for TestSprite: https://github.com/TestSprite/testsprite-cli

Visit AISeeKing: https://www.youtube.com/@aiseeking

In this video, I'll be covering all the major Claude Code upgrades released over the past two months, including Claude Opus 5, cross-session messaging, the new Design command, fork mode, automated permissions, security scanning, and more. I'll also explain why Anthropic's permanent 25% weekly-limit increase is actually a 17% reduction compared to the limits users have today.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Claude Opus 5 is now the default Opus model in Claude Code and supports a one-million-token context window on eligible plans.
🎨 The new Design command creates editable UI artboards before Claude implements your chosen design.
🔗 Cross-session messaging allows multiple Claude Code sessions to communicate and coordinate their work.
🤖 Fork mode can launch background subagents w

items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. I know that this is a claude code update video, but if you're a codeex snob instead, then I have good news for you because I have done a similar codeex update video on my other channel, AIC King. So, you can check that out. Also, subscribe to that channel because there's some good content coming over there as well. Link in the description. So, it's been about 2 months since I properly covered claude code and Anthropic has been shipping like crazy. There's a new Opus model. Sessions can now talk to each other. Auto mode is now the default. And there's a new design skill as well. But there's also some rate limit drama because of course there is. Anthropic just announced what they're calling a permanent 25% increase to weekly limits. But if you do the math, it's actually a 17% cut compared to what you're getting right now. Classic. We'll get to that at the end. So, let's get right into it. Before we dive in, let me tell you something. Boris Churnney built Claude code and he said something that stuck with me. He doesn't write the prompts anymore. The loop does. His job is to write the loop. A loop acts, observes a real signal, decides what to do next, and repeats until a goal actually holds. Five blocks, trigger, goal, the work, memory, and verification. The feedback gate, the one block allowed to say, "No, not done yet." Everyone tunes the model and the prompt. Almost nobody builds this block. And in 2026, your loop is only as good as its feedback gate. Here's what that cost me. I had a loop running for two days. Test screen every single iteration. I came back to it proud of myself. Opened the app and the whole checkout flow was dead button. Did nothing. No error. Just dead. The agent had been running unit tests against its own mocks the entire time. Green on its own machine, reporting done on something no real user could actually use. A green run on the agent's own machine proves nothing. So the question I got stuck on is what's the one signal that actually closes the loop? And it's the boring answer. The deployed thing behaving for a real user. That's the block I tell you to obsess over. The verifier I use is open source, the test sprite CLI. The agent calls it midbuild and it drives the live app like a real user would, not Mox. The actual deployed thing. When it broke that checkout flow again, it didn't just say failed. It handed back a screenshot of exactly what the user would have seen. The dead button frozen. The agent read that patched it, reran. I wasn't in the loop for any of it. That's what a closed loop actually feels like. Not a bigger brain, a stricter referee. The model isn't your bottleneck anymore. The loop is, and the loop is only as good as what's allowed to tell it no. If you want to start using it, then the installation process is very simple. You'll need node 20.19, 22.13, or 24 and up. Install with npm installg at testrite/estrite cli. Grab your API key from the dashboard under settings API keys. Copy it. It only shows once. Run test setup. Paste your key in. Then confirm everything's connected with test sprite o status. That's it. You're ready to go. So when you design your next one, don't start with the model. Start with the verifier. For me, that's test sprite open source Apache 2.0. Links below. First up, the big one. Claude Opus 5 is now the default Opus model in Claude Code. It rolled out in late July and it's the default on max team premium enterprise pay as you go and the API. The headline feature here is that it runs with a 1 million token context window on the API and on the max team and enterprise plans which is huge for large code bases. Fast mode has also moved over to Opus 5 at $10 input and $50 output per million tokens. You can switch to it by running the model command and picking it from the picker or just typing /modclaw-opus-5 from my usage so far. It's a noticeable step up from opus 4.8 especially on long agentic tasks where the old models would start losing the plot. Now let's talk about the features because there are a lot of them. The newest one is the /design command which is in research preview right now. This basically brings claude design's artboard workflow right into the CLI and the desktop app. You run slashdesign with a brief like redesign the composer and Claude publishes a canvas of editable artboards for your UI. You open the link, pick the option you like, tweak it, and then tell Claude to implement that one. It's available on Promax Team and Enterprise. I've played with it a bit and for front-end work, this is actually a pretty nice workflow. Instead of Claude guessing what you want, you get options to pick from. This is quite great to see. Next, cross- session messaging. So your clawed code sessions can now message each other. If you have two sessions open on the same machine, one session can discover the others and send them messages. So if you change a database column in one session, you can just say tell the session working on the payments API that this column got renamed and it does it. You can also just type the at@ symbol in the prompt to mention another session by name. It started on Mac OS and Linux in early August and it's on native Windows now as well. This is kind of awesome for anyone who runs multiple sessions in parallel, which let's be honest is most of us at this point. Related to that, fork mode is now on by default. This means Claude can spin up a sub agent that inherits the full conversation and the prompt cache instead of starting fresh, so you don't have to reexplain everything for a side task. You can trigger it yourself with a slubtask command like slubtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far. The fork runs in the background and the result drops back into your conversation when it's done. They've also removed the 200 sub agent per session cap and sessions now run up to 20 sub aents concurrently by default. So the whole multi-agent thing is getting pushed really hard. Now the more controversial one, auto mode became the default permission mode for new sessions on Pro Max and team plans starting August 14th. So instead of asking you for permission on every action, a classifier runs in the background. lets safe actions through and blocks the risky ones. If you had set your own default mode, it stays in place unless you accept the switch prompt. Personally, I've been running auto mode for a while, and it's fine for most work, but I know some people don't love a classifier making these calls. The good news is that the classifier calls no longer count toward your usage limits, which used to be a hidden tax on this mode. You can still switch modes anytime, so there's that. The desktop app also got some love. Claude Code Desktop now has a built-in browser, so Claude can pull up docs or designs and interact with pages the same way it does with your local dev server previews. And on Mac OS, there's now an iOS simulator pane in public beta. When Claude builds and launches your app in the simulator, the pane opens next to the conversation and streams the device screen live, so you can literally watch Claude tap through your app to verify its changes. For anyone doing iOS development, this is pretty amazing, to be honest. There's also a new Claude security plugin from Anthropic. It runs a multi-agent vulnerability scan of your codebase. Agents map your architecture, build a threat model, hunt for vulnerabilities, and independently review every finding before writing a report. You can scan a whole repo, just a branches, diff, a PR, or a single commit, and then turn the findings into patches that you review and apply yourself. You install it with /plugin installclaude-curity at claude-plugins-official. I ran it on one of my projects and it found a couple of real issues, so it's not just marketing flop. On the code review side, /code-review now runs as a background sub aent with its own context window. So the review work stays out of your conversation and the findings arrive when it's done. And / review is now an alias for it, which is nice. A few more quick ones. There's a new concise output style that makes Claude lead with the result and skip all the preamble, which you can turn on in the config menu. Remote control is now out of research preview and any machine running Claude remote control shows up as a device card in the Claude mobile app. So you can start a session on your desktop right from your phone. GitLab users finally got proper support. So merge request URLs work with the-workree flag and plug-in marketplaces can clone from gitlab.com. There's a new /docctor command that diagnoses setup issues and can fix them. There's a screen reader mode for accessibility and there's a new environment variable called anthropic debro_model that sets which model new sessions start on. Self-hosted environments are also in public beta on team and enterprise. So cloud sessions can run on your own infrastructure inside your own network. So that's a genuinely massive amount of shipping in 2 months. But now let's talk about the rate limits because this is where it gets spicy. Quick recap first. Back in May, Anthropic doubled the 5-hour session limits and removed the peak hour throttling thanks to all that new compute they got from the SpaceX Colossus deal. They also boosted the weekly limits by 50% as a temporary thing. And they kept extending it over and over through July 13th, then July 19th, then August 19th, and then August 31, always saying they hope to make it permanent. Well, on August 30th, we got the answer. Starting September 14th, the standard weekly limits go up by a permanent 25% on pro, max, team, and seat-based enterprise. Sounds great, right? Except the temporary 50% boost ends on September 13th. So, if your baseline was 100 units, you're currently getting 150 and after September 14th, you'll get a 125. That is a 17% cut compared to what you have today, dressed up as a 25% increase. And the funny part is Anthropic actually posted the announcement, then deleted it and reposted a clarified version where they admitted, and I quote, "Compared to today, this works out to a 17% reduction in weekly limits." They also teased some exciting changes coming for more visibility and control of your usage. So, at least they came clean about the math, but the framing was not great. Now, to be fair, a permanent 25% increase over the original baseline is still better than the boost just expiring completely, which was the other possibility. and the doubled 5-hour limits from May are staying. Plus, there are some small cushions. Now, Claude Code can autocontin your session when a usage limit resets, both in the CLI and with a checkbox on the desktop limit card, so you don't have to babysit the timer. The auto mode classifier calls don't count against you anymore. And if you really need more, you can enable usage credits past your cap at API rates. But if you're a heavy user who got used to the boosted limits over the last 4 months, September 14th is going to feel like a nerf because it is one. If you ask me, they should have just called it what it is from day one. People don't mind limits nearly as much as they mind being told a cut is an increase. Overall though, looking at these two months as a whole, the feature velocity is honestly impressive. Opus 5 with the 1 million context cross session messaging, the design skill, the security plugin. Claude Code is pulling further ahead of the competition on features and the limit situation while annoying is still better than the original baseline. So, it's a mixed bag, but mostly a good one. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments.
